title: Mass-anisotropy driven stripe pattern formation and directional modulational instability in polariton condensate
authors: Hari Sadhan Ghosh, Soumyadeep Halder, Subrata Das, Sonjoy Majumder
abstract: Motivated by recent experimental advances toward electrical control of the effective mass and the realization of anisotropic mass distributions, we investigate the impact of mass anisotropy on driven-dissipative polariton condensates, focusing on modulational instability, pattern formation, and the collective dynamics of the emergent patterns. We show that unequal effective masses along the two orthogonal directions induce stripe pattern formation in an exciton-polariton condensate pumped by a non-resonant Gaussian laser beam above a critical mass ratio. A Bogoliubov analysis of the homogeneously pumped system reveals that mass anisotropy leaves the modulational-instability criteria unchanged but reshapes the unstable-mode dispersion by reducing the most unstable wave- length along the direction of larger effective mass with increasing mass ratio. This introduces an anisotropy-controlled length scale for pattern selection. When the pump width becomes comparable to the most unstable wavelength, the condensate becomes modulationally unstable and develops stripe patterns along the direction of larger effective mass, accompanied by particle-number fluctua- tions and center-of-mass oscillations along the same direction. As the pump width increases further, the stripes become distorted and develop spatial irregularities during the time evolution, indicative of modulational instability. Nevertheless, the anisotropic mass distribution preserves a pronounced directional preference, in contrast to the fully disordered patterns observed in the isotropic-mass case. Our results identify mass anisotropy as a key control parameter for directional modulational instability and pattern formation in nonequilibrium polariton condensates.
summary: This paper explores how tuning the mass anisotropy in polariton condensates controls their pattern formation and stability. By analyzing the system's linear excitations, the authors show that unequal effective masses induce stable, directionally preferred stripe patterns. This establishes mass anisotropy as a powerful control knob for directional instability in these non-equilibrium quantum systems.
main_problem: The study investigates how mass anisotropy affects modulational instability, pattern formation, and collective dynamics in driven-dissipative polariton condensates.
main_result: Mass anisotropy is identified as a key control parameter, inducing stripe patterns along the direction of the greater effective mass, which is a directional effect absent in isotropic systems.
method: The analysis employs linear stability analysis using the Bogoliubov-de Gennes approximation on the open-dissipative Gross-Pitaevskii equation.
model_or_system: The system is an exciton-polariton condensate, modeled as a driven-dissipative system with an effective mass that can be tuned to exhibit anisotropy.
key_observables: Stripe pattern formation, center-of-mass oscillations, most unstable wavelength ($\lambda_m$), and the imaginary part of the Bogoliubov spectrum ($	ext{Im } \omega_k$).
important_parameters: Mass anisotropy ratio ($m_y/m_x$), pump power ($P$), and pump width ($\sigma$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on a small perturbation approximation around the steady state and uses a mean-field description.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the Bogoliubov spectrum showing instability regions, and time evolution plots demonstrate the formation of anisotropic stripe patterns and oscillations.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by establishing the governing equations and performing linear stability analysis to determine instability criteria, followed by numerical simulations to observe pattern formation and directional dynamics.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses non-equilibrium many-body dynamics in an optical cavity setting, providing a clear mechanism (mass anisotropy) to control pattern selection and directional instabilities, which is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems.
